explain.summary: A new memory fades over time unless it is used again. Ines crammed 2 hours in one night, so her memory of the words was strong the next morning but faded fast. Her brother spread the same 2 hours over six days, with sleep in between, so he pulled each word back up again and again — and every time made the memory last longer.
rules: How much she learns at first depends on study time, number of words and how fast she learns.
After that, what she remembers fades by half over a 'half-life' of a few days.
Each extra day the study is spread over makes that half-life about 1.5 times longer.
Less sleep than 8 hours makes the half-life shorter; more sleep makes it a little longer.
The surprise-quiz score is what's left after the wait.

source.fact: A 2013 review of ten study techniques rated two as most effective: spreading study out over time (distributed practice) and quizzing yourself (practice testing).
A review of 317 experiments found that the gap between study sessions and the time until the test work together: the best gap gets longer the longer you need to remember.
Sleep after learning helps save new information in the brain; learning ability may drop by up to 40% without sleep, and you can't pull an all-nighter and still learn effectively.
Teens aged 13–17 need 8–10 hours of sleep a day.
A modern repeat of Ebbinghaus's famous 1880s memory experiment reproduced his forgetting curve, with a possible upward jump at the 24-hour point that may be linked to sleep.

choice.what: Forgetting halves memory over a fixed half-life
choice.why: Real forgetting curves drop fast at first and then slow down; a halving curve has that shape and is easy to read.

choice.what: Each extra day of spacing makes the half-life 1.5 times longer
choice.why: Chosen so the model reproduces the twins' week-later scores (about 12 and 34 words). The real benefit of spacing depends on the material and the person.

choice.what: Sleep changes the half-life smoothly around 8 hours
choice.why: Sources agree sleep strengthens memories but don't give one formula, so we used a gentle curve.

choice.what: Learning speed only changes how much she learns at first
choice.why: This keeps the 'worse at languages' test clear: a slower learner would score lower the very next morning.

choice.what: It takes about 2.5 minutes of study per word to learn it fully
choice.why: A round number so 40 words in 2 hours are all learned by the next morning, as in the case.

illustrative: Ines and her brother are fictional; their scores (12 and 34 words a week later) are made up to fit the model.
The 4-day half-life after cramming is an illustrative value, not a measurement.
provenance.studying: Scientists are still working out exactly why spaced practice works so well, and exactly how the sleeping brain chooses which memories to keep.

citations.title: Which Study Strategies Make the Grade?
citations.supports: Reports a 2013 review (Dunlosky and colleagues) in which practice testing and distributed practice were the only two techniques rated highly effective; spreading study over time boosts performance across many kinds of tests.

citations.title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis (Psychological Bulletin)
citations.supports: Meta-analysis of 839 assessments from 317 experiments; the gap between study sessions and the retention interval jointly affect recall, and the best gap increases as the retention interval increases.

citations.title: Sleep On It: How Snoozing Strengthens Your Memory
citations.supports: Sleep after learning is essential to save new information in the brain; learning ability may drop by up to 40% without sleep; 'You can't pull an all-nighter and still learn effectively.'

citations.title: About Sleep
citations.supports: Recommended sleep: teens 13–17 years need 8–10 hours per day; school-age children 6–12 need 9–12 hours.

citations.title: Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve
citations.supports: Murre and Dros successfully replicated Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve; the curve is not completely smooth and probably shows an upward jump starting at the 24-hour point.

does: Shows a memory fading fast after cramming and lasting much longer when the same study time is spread out
Shows sleep between sessions making memories last longer
Lets you test whether 'just a slower learner' fits the evidence
doesnt: Measure any real person — Ines is fictional and the numbers are illustrative
Include quizzing yourself, how interesting the words are, or stress
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If you often can't sleep, or school stress feels too big, talk with an adult you trust.
